Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. There have been discussions at the staff level. I would like to inquire of the opposition Parties, for the record, whether or not it would be possible to complete all stages of this important Bill to provide for the resumption and continuation of postal services today. Government Members are prepared to stay as late as necessary to complete this matter despite the fact that this is Thanksgiving weekend and Members are wanting to return to their ridings.
We have arranged for the Senate to sit at two o'clock this afternoon in order that it can deal with the matter. We might possibly get Royal Assent if we have the co-operation of all Parties.
It is the Government's wish to resolve this matter so there can be as little inconvenience as possible to the public and that any further violence on the picket lines can be restricted.
I inquire once again of the opposition Parties whether it is possible to complete all stages of this Bill today.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise to speak on second reading of Bill C-86, the Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987. As the

October 9, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
title of the Bill suggests, its prime purpose is to order a resumption of full mail and other postal services across the country.
Hon. Members will be well aware that these services have been disrupted for the second time in less than four months as a result of a labour dispute and work stoppages. On this occasion the labour dispute involves the Canadian Union of Postal Workers representing some 23,000 inside postal workers employed by the Canada Post Corporation.
The spectre of a protracted and damaging test of economic strength between the corporation and the union is now selfevident. Unfortunately, these two combatants have the capacity to inflict more punishment on third parties than on each other. The Government is not prepared to stand idly by and permit a gradual deterioration of postal services through escalating rotating strikes.

subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Members of the House are fully aware of the inherent dangers and the potential for violence in the type of contest in which these two parties are engaged. Our industrial relations system certainly permits a test of economic strength between disputant unions and corporations.

However, Mr. Speaker, when there is a situation, such as we have here, with a potential for disorder on a national scale, government must become the defender of the public interest and know when to say enough is enough. This is particularly true when there is no hope for a settlement through the collective bargaining process.
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of any expectation for an early negotiated settlement, we are therefore acting decisively to terminate what commissioner Foisy apprehensively predicted as the "battle of the titans".
The bill before the House provides for the termination of all work stoppages and established procedures for the settlement of the labour dispute.

Before dealing in greater detail with the provisions of the Bill, I want to address certain considerations. In this context, I am conscious of the fact that I rose in this House just over a month ago in late August to introduce a similar Bill dealing on that occasion with a crippling national railway strike.
As I believe I indicated to Hon. Members during the debate on that Bill, I take no pleasure in introducing back-to-work legislation. Such legislation represents an abdication by the parties of their responsibility to resolve their own differences.
The Government's general policy is not to intervene in labour negotiations between the parties other than by the well tried and usually effective mechanisms of conciliation and mediation. We are proud of the record in federal jurisdiction where consistently in excess of 90 per cent of collective
agreements are renewed without resort to work stoppages. However, the federal labour relations jurisdiction covered by Part V of the Code includes some vital and sensitive industries. Work stoppages in some of these industries are capable of inflicting greater damage more rapidly on innocent third parties than they inflict on either of the parties directly involved.
In these sensitive and vital industries, it is particularly incumbent on the parties that they meet their responsibilities to negotiate their own settlements. It may require considerable skill and flexibility to do so but they owe nothing less to the Canadians they serve.
It is this Government's preference by far not to intervene through special legislation in labour disputes. However, neither employers nor trade unions in the federal labour jurisdiction should be under an illusion as to our determination to act when private disputes are inflicting public damage.
One further word of caution is perhaps necessary. Federal jurisdiction employers and trade unions should not take this express willingness by the Government to act when circumstances so dictate as an invitation to shirk their respective responsibilities and to propel their labour disputes into Parliament. The parties should not seek to monopolize the valuable time of the House or try the patience of Parliament by confronting us with the need to settle one labour dispute after another. If there is any tendency or sign of a trend in this direction, the parties should be warned that they may provoke more far-reaching and unpalatable remedies than they had anticipated.

A second general consideration I would like to touch on, Mr. Speaker, concerns the evolution of the Canada Post Corporation. It is, I am sure, a subject that other Hon. Members will want to address and will no doubt do so at greater length. When the Canada Post Corporation Act was proclaimed in October, 1981, there was a general expectation that the transformation from a government department would give the new corporation the capacity to function in the marketplace in a way that was not previously possible.
Indeed, I believe that these sentiments echo or at least paraphrase the words expressed at the time by those reponsible for introducing the enabling legislation. When this government came into office, it was far from clear that any positive transformation had occurred. Service levels remained poor and deficits continued to bedevil the corporation.

What the Government did was to insist that the corporation improve its service standards and its financial performance. The message was clear. The umbilical cord was to be cut and the flow of general Government subsidies was to be halted. The corporation had to become viable and to act in very large measure as a commercial enterprise.
October 9, 1987

Naturally, the approach implied change and change implied, among other things, labour relation issues. It became the responsibility of corporation management and the unions representing its employees to address these issues. It seems in the present case that they have been unable to do so without confrontation and disruption of mail services. That situation is, to say the least, disappointing.
It may be a truism, but organizations that fail to change with the times are left behind the times. The transformation of the Canada Post Corporation into an efficient and viable enterprise calls for flexibility and a willingness to adapt on the the part of both management and labour. With such flexibility and readiness to attack-to adapt, the future of the corporation and its employees-

With such flexibility and readiness to adapt, the future of the corporation and its employees is best assured. Without these qualities, the future for both is bleak.

This brings me, Mr. Speaker, close to the cause of these present proceedings before the House, namely labour relations at the Canada Post Corporation. I could dig back over the past twenty years or more and recite the litany of labour disputes and major confrontations involving the former Post Office Department and now the Corporation. Instead, Mr. Speaker, I will limit myself to two or three more recent assessments of the state of the labour-management relationship.
The review committee on the mandate and productivity of the Canada Post Corporation, known as the Marchment Committee. Indicated that it had never seen labour relations as acrimonious as those that exist between the corporation and its unions.
Mr. Speaker, the committee further characterized the relationship as poisonous to the point of the potential destruction of the enterprise. More recently, Kenneth Swan, the conciliation commissioner in the dispute between the Corporation and the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada, found that the relationships of the representatives of the parties have deteriorated to the point where they are intensely personal and bitter. In the present dispute, conciliation commissioner Claude Foisy observed, at the outset of his report, that the relations between the parties were marked by a profound mutual distrust.
Mr. Speaker, this sorry story would be bad enough, if it only involved the parties themselves. Unfortunately, it does not. It also involves the effectiveness of a service on which Canadians sould be able to rely with greater assurance. That, Mr. Speaker is among the reasons that we find ourselves dealing with Bill C-86 in the House today.
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
Let me now turn to the specifics of the current dispute between the corporation and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers representing some 23,000 inside workers. The collective agreement between the parties expired just over a year ago, on September 30, 1986. A notice of dispute was received from the union on October 26, 1986, and I responded with the appointment of a staff conciliation officer on October 30. The conciliation officer, Mr. Andre Drouin, met with the parties on several occasions over the next three months or so. However, the parties were unable to reach agreement despite his assistance.
When the officer reported out of the case it was clear that virtually all key issues remained in dispute. In the circumstances I exercised the discretion granted to me under the Canada Labour Code to provide for a further and more formal level of conciliation. In this regard I appointed Claude H. Foisy, Q.C., of Mount-Royal, Quebec, as conciliation commissioner on February 23, 1987. Mr. Foisy is an experienced labour relations practitioner, a former vice-chairman of the Canada Labour Relations Board, and now a respected labour arbitrator and conciliator in private practice.
Mr. Foisy held a series of meetings with the parties over a period of some Five months from early March to mid-August. I gather he was inundated with briefs and position papers. However, as indicated in his report, he found it difficult to engage the parties in a genuine dialogue on the major items in dispute. Eventually he concluded that settlement was not possible in negotiations under his auspices and he withdrew to write his report and recommendations.
I released Mr. Foisy's report to the parties on the morning of September 22, 1987, and released it publicly later the same day. The report is comprehensive if not exhaustive. Covering in excess of 80 pages it deals with the background to the dispute and focuses, at the parties' request, on the key issues in contention. The commissioner endeavoured to assess the competing demands and interests of the parties. He recognized, on the one hand, the legitimate requirements of the corporation to perform as a viable business, but never neglected the need to provide appropriate protection for the corporation's existing employees.
The objective of the report's contents was perhaps best illustrated by the initial reactions expressed by the parties. I understand the corporation's spokesman referred in radio news clips to "this balanced report". The union in its initial press statement indicated that:
Commissioner Foisy made some recommendations that reflect our demands,
some recommendations that reflect the employer's, some other that go half
way for both and others which are not addressed.
Turning to Commissioner Foisy's recommendations, he classified them under four headings: job security, demands affecting operations, grievance and arbitration procedures, and health and safety. Under the job security heading the report

October 9, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
addresses the high profile franchising issue. The union demand in this area called for a modification of the existing contracting-out provision of the collective agreement so as to prevent the loss of bargaining unit work through the awarding of franchises and the opening of new sub post offices.
Over all, the commissioner's report recognizes the legitimate interests of the union in wanting to negotiate the maintenance of desirable counter jobs but also recognizes the corporation's legitimate interest in wanting to deal with the private sector. In the circumstances, there is no recommendation in favour of modifying the present contracting-out provision. What the report recommends instead is special and comprehensive employment protection and financial compensation for the life of the agreement for members of the bargaining unit who currently work at post office counters.

I have raised this matter, Mr. Speaker, because I believe that the commissioner's examination of the job security issue, as it relates to franchising and private sector sub-post offices, illustrates two important points.
First, I believe that it shows the efforts which have been made to reconcile the competing demands of the parties. Secondly, the recommendation shows that the need to adapt to change does not have to be accomplished at the expense of existing employees.
The same elements are found elsewhere in the report. For example, in the area of part-time work, the corporation would be accorded greater flexibility to use part-timers in meeting its service targets. However, the current ceiling on the part-time employment complement would be maintained.

Following release of the conciliation commissioner's report, the parties had before them a reasoned and reasonable document which should have served as a basis for negotiations towards settlement. Instead, the negotiations deteriorated. Consequently, on September 29, I asked my Associate Deputy Minister, Bill Kelly, to meet with the parties to assess what progress had been made since the release of Commissioner Foisy's report, how far the parties were apart, their willingness to compromise, and whether in his view this dispute could be resolved through the collective bargaining process short of a protracted strike with all its inherent dangers.
Mr. Kelly advised me that the parties had made no progress on the major issues in this dispute since the release of the conciliation commissioner's report on September 22, 1987. He also provided me with his judgment, resulting from private discussions with both sides, that this dispute could not be resolved through the collective bargaining process short of a lengthy test of economic strength. I have complete confidence in Mr. Kelly's judgment in such matters and I am sure Hon. Members share my opinion of his abilities. He has demonstrated the capacity to get to the root of issues and find avenues for settlement which others thought did not exist. While I found
no consolation in the assessment Mr. Kelly gave me, I had no doubt as to its accuracy.

Mr. Speaker, I publicly urged the parties to return to the bargaining table. However, in the light of the assessment I had received, I also gave them notice that the government would not tolerate a protracted and disruptive work stoppage at Canada Post. I had hoped, Mr. Speaker, that the warning would stimulate serious efforts at settlement.
Instead, what appears to have been a somewhat desultory meeting, on lesser issues, took place last Sunday. Then, on Monday, when it was fully expected that more intensive negotiations would commence, the parties could only manage a brief two hour session. They emerged from this meeting indicating how far they were apart and emphasizing how entrenched they were on key issues.
At that point, Mr. Speaker, I gave the parties formal notice that the break off of negotiations last monday, after a mere two hours, was unacceptable to the Canadian public. In a telegram to both sides, I warned them that, if they were incapable of resolving the dispute, through collective bargaining, the government would lift the responsibility from their shoulders.
In my telegram, Mr. Speaker, I also indicated my intention to give notice in the House of Commons which would enable the government to introduce legislation to resolve the dispute.
I effectively challenged the parties to remove the need for legislation by showing the will and the capacity to achieve a resolution through collective bargaining. Mr. Speaker, they did not rise to the challenge.
With no settlement in sight and with Canadians faced with the disruption of mail services for the second time within four months, the Government decided to act. We have tabled legislation which, as I shall explain shortly, offers the parties the opportunity to settle their differences in mediation, but not while they hold up the Canadian public for ransom.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
In tabling this legislation our message is very clear. The Government will not allow the mail to be disrupted again this year. It will not stand by while the adverse impact builds just because the Canada Post Corporation and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers cannot settle their dispute without inflicting damage on the Canadian public.
I turn now to the provisions of the Bill before the House. In the first instance, and as a first priority, the Bill provides for the immediate termination of the work stoppages and the resumption of postal services. The Bill also provides for the extension of the collective agreement for a period to be determined through arbitration, if necessary, of not less than
October 9, 1987

two and not more than three years. Additionally, the Bill provides for the settlement of the issues in dispute through the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator.

I have already dealt with the rationale for terminating the work stoppage and ordering a resumption of full postal operations. The Canadian economy cannot be subjected to a second postal work stoppage within four months from the previous strike. What I want to emphasize most at this point, Mr. Speaker, is the importance I attach to the provision which the bill makes for the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator.
The parties in this dispute are no strangers to protracted negotiations and work stoppages. In 1981, Mr. Speaker, Canadians were subjected to a lengthy strike of inside postal workers and were without mail for six weeks. Canadians were kept waiting for a total of forty-two days before labour and management could settle their differences through economic sanctions.

In the present dispute the corporation and the union have been bargaining for more than a year and are well aware of the issues. They have had the benefit of conciliation officer assistance followed by a second stage of conciliation with a conciliation commissioner. This second stage was unsuccessful and led to the report and recommendations of Commissioner Foisy. The report and recommendations should have set the scene for negotiations toward settlement.

After I released Mr. Foisy's report, Mr. Speaker, the onus for settlement rested squarely on the parties' shoulders. I had no intention of transferring this responsibility to a mediator. To have done so would have provided the parties with a sanctuary from public opinion during a protracted mediation process while they continued on the path of mutually assured destruction.

Against this background the Bill before the House provides for the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator rather than strict arbitration. This is done with the express purpose of affording the parties one last chance to do it for themselves. However, while they are attempting to settle their differences they will not be in a position to pursue their diversionary tactics against each other.
On this occasion the Government does not intend to let matters drag on. The parties are guaranteed the opportunity of mediation, but not at the expense of the economy and public interest. I sincerely hope that they will arrive at their own agreement with the assistance of the mediator-arbitrator. If they have their own best interests at heart they should seize this opportunity to do so. At the same time they just may lay the foundation for a much needed improved future relationship. However, should the parties fail yet again, the mediator-arbitrator will be empowered to make binding decisions.
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987 [Translation]
I will conclude at this point, Mr. Speaker, because as I indicated before I know that several other members will want to speak to this Bill. But before I conclude, allow me to add that there had been some reason to hope that labour relations at the Canada Post Corporation would improve. However, it proved to be a false hope, Mr. Speaker. Confrontation was never far away even when agreements were reached. Each round of bargaining brought its threats to the provision of these important postal services. This past summer an overt and violent conflict occurred. This government will not tolerate yet another disruption of the mail.

We decided to act firmly and decisively. Let there be no doubt in this House that when a private clash of wills takes precedence over the public interest the Government will not hesitate to intervene.

Mr. Speaker, I rise very reluctantly in the House today, to address, on behalf of my Party, the Bill tabled for our consideration, Bill C-86, whose purpose is to provide for the normal resumption of postal services but whose hidden objective is to break a strike.

What puzzles me is, first, the disturbing way in which the Government has asked the opposition Parties for co-operation. When the Minister rose in the House to ask for all-Party agreement to pass this Bill through all stages today I made a few remarks explaining that when the Bill was tabled in the House yesterday we had not been consulted. The Government had decided to push aside the normal tradition of a gentlemen's agreement between House Leaders to try to reach agreement on pieces of legislation. This has worked many times recently and over the years. For the Government to table a piece of legislation in the House of Commons and for the Minister to ask us to start negotiating in public is baloney. It means, in my opinion-

In your opinion?

Yes, in my humble opinion it means that the Minister is not seriously trying to reach an agreement to pass this Bill rapidly.
I am not sure that this Bill has to be passed rapidly anyway, because in my opinion it is an ill-advised piece of legislation. It flies in the face of our Canadian tradition of trying to settle labour disputes through bargaining.
The Minister spent most of the time during his speech explaining to us that bargaining was not working in this case. That is surprising because we saw a similar situation in June when the letter carriers were on strike with the Post Office. The strike was settled by negotiation. The parties came to an agreement after the Government appointed a mediator. While the Government first refused to appoint a mediator and only saw the light a week later, I must give credit to the Government for finally appointing a mediator which resulted in the parties coming to an agreement peacefully and ending the strike.
Why must the Government use the ballistic approach this time to try to bring the parties together? I am simply saying that it will be much more difficult and this action shows the image of the Government.
Not only is this piece of legislation ill advised, it is premature. There is no national emergency. We all remember the rail strike. In that case, grain was not moving, coal was not moving, and other commodities were not moving across the country. A rail strike presented the possibility of severely crippling the Canadian economy. Such is not the case with this strike. There were rotating strikes and the mail, by and large, was moving. There is no national emergency and this Bill is premature.
[ Translation]
In fact, what we have seen and what we are still seeing is a series of rotating strikes across this country. We do not have a national strike from sea to sea, bringing mail delivery to a complete standstill. That is not the case. However, since the Minister tabled his Bill and, in doing so, provoked the urath of postal workers, there is a very real threat that the rotating strikes will gradually turn into a full-blown national strike, and if that is what the Government wants, that is probably what it is going to get. However, if this happens, I can inform the Government we will hold it responsible for escalating a strike that was relatively peaceful.
Even according to the Minister responsible for Canada Post, who brags about it daily, mail delivery is proceeding almost normally. I was reading some reports not long ago in which postal officials said that the volume of mail being processed today is 1.8 percent greater than the volume processed by the Canada Post Corporation a year ago. So our postal services are operating, despite the rotating strikes, and the Government had no business bringing in a Bill prematurely, which will only lead to provocation, especially since negotiations were
proceeding and representatives for Canada Post employees had decided recently to make a major concession with respect to privatization, which, as we all know, has been the main stumbling block in the negotiations.
The president of the union mentioned recently that he was opening the door to the Corporation's plan to set up postal franchises. Obviously, he was doing so on certain conditions. He wanted to ensure that this would be done mostly in new developments. He didn't want existing post offices to be shut down and replaced by wickets in drugstores and supermarkets, with people being paid the minimum wage, while postal employees earned decent wages.
Certain terms could certainly have been negotiated, and the union representative had seriously opened the door to a resumption of the negotiations by giving ground on the main demands of Canada Post. The Government therefore chose the worst possible moment to introduce such repressive legislation. A negotiated settlement achieved at the bargaining table is always better than an imposed one, just as an out of court settlement is always preferable in civil proceedings. I do not know why the Government cannot understand this principle, even though some of its own members do. Recently, the Hon. Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon) paid more than lip service to this concept by joining the picket line. Let me tell you why, and I would like to quote what he said. According to an article in Le Journal de Montreal, the purpose of his gesture was to denounce the anti-social attitude of his Government. This is what the Conservative Member for Richelieu did.
He stated that he was against the hiring of strikebreakers. He saw this provocation. He also expressed serious reservations about back-to-work legislation, and this was before the Bill was introduced. He had already understood-

The Hon. Members opposite do not like to hear this. They are always interrupting. I am anxious to see them rise to defend their views as their colleague for Richelieu has had the courage to do.
If we look at the basic arguments of the Hon. Member, who is a Conservative, we find that he said that the workers have the right to strike and that the conflict should be allowed to resolve itself normally as the national interest is not being threatened. I am therefore not the only one to say so. The national interest is not being threatened and the rotating strikes have not caused any real acts of violence, at least until now.
Mr. Speaker, all this goes to show that, as surprising as it may seem, some of the Conservative Members understand reason. Some of them have the courage to rise publicly to express their views. What is at issue here is what is happening to the collective bargaining system in Canada now that we have a Bill which plainly interferes with a strike which is quite legal and which complies with all the rules. Such special
October 9, 1987

legislation seems totally at variance with the principles supposedly supported by the Government, and especially by the Prime Minister who, at other times, and he would not do so in the House now, likes to say that he is on the side of the workers and of collective bargaining.
As recently as July 29, the Prime Minister wrote a letter to Mrs. Shirley Carr, President of the Canadian Labour Congress, in which he said the following. As the letter was in English, I shall change over to the language of Shakespeare:

"The existing framework for collective bargaining has again proven its capacity to bring employers and bargaining agents to resolve even the most difficult disputes without government interference". I would like the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to return to the House today and repeat that sentence. However, I know he is busy and that is why I have offered to speak on his behalf and remind Canadians of what he is saying while already campaigning for the next election. I am not saying either that he is wrong in beginning the campaign early.
Let me continue to quote the Prime Minister about bargaining settlements. He said, "Such settlements are better by far than any that would be imposed through legislation". That is what I said earlier, yet 1 was heckled by my colleagues opposite. 1 do not know if they will heckle their own leader, but 1 was repeating exactly what the Prime Minister was thinking when he was speaking. However, the Prime Minister and the Government have the bad habit of saying something to please some people but doing the exact opposite the next day, probably to please another group of people.

Mr. Speaker, the Government is responsible for this strike and, although it might surprise some Canadians who hear me say that, I will explain why. It is the Government, with the last Budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), which has put Canada Post in a straight jacket. In all fairness, we certainly cannot blame the Canada Post Corporation and its negotiators who are doing their best, within of course the limited means available to them.
Under the plan imposed by the Minister of Finance for a balanced budget by next spring Canada Post Corporation finds it very difficult to operate and, under the circumstances, it has no other alternative but to make cuts and more cuts. The Canada Post Corporation is forced to franchise and privatize its operations, to apply the axe to the job security of postal workers, men and women, to meet the financial demands of the Government. That is why I say that the Government is responsible for this strike.
The Government has caused the strike with its postal service privatization plan which these working men and women are opposed to because they see it as a threat to their job security. Nobody likes to lose his or her job or to approve in advance plans which will likely result in job losses. That is why postal

working men and women are fighting back, for their livelihood is at stake.
I was looking for instance at our friend Bill Kelly, the Deputy Minister. The Minister answered the Hon. Member had not read his press release, issued that morning, and everything was in there.
I had read the press release, but the problem is that in that release it was impossible to determine what Mr. Bill Kelly, the Deputy Minister of Labour, was doing there.
One thing we did understand about the press release, and it was that Mr. Kelly was not there as a mediator. And that was the Government's big mistake.
I would like to add that the Government is sending the wrong signal with this back-to-work legislation. Canada Post was already strapped for funds because of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and because of decisions made in Cabinet. Canada Post now has a clear signal that it does not have to negotiate. The back-to-work legislation is there. The employees will have to return to work and do their jobs. Why would the officers of Canada Post bend over backward and start conceding on various fronts around the table? They do not have to do that. The message is loud and clear. It is there; the writing is on the wall.

Why Bill C-86, Mr. Speaker? The Minister claims it is in order to end the strike because it jeopardizes mail delivery, but that is not even true-mail is being distributed. There must be an underlying reason, there is something fishy going on. And I will suggest two possible reasons for this shotgun approach taken by the government.
The first reason in my view is that here is a government whose popularity is on a constant downslide, as indicated by opinion polls, and it must try behind closed doors, in its strategy meetings, to find new methods to beef up its image. A good right-using attitude for a Conservative government is to say: We will look tough with workers. That will work. Then people will say we are in charge.
I, for one, say that holding Canadian workers to ransom is not the right way for a government to enhance its image when it is already very damaged.
Besides, there are other reasons as well. It may not only be a tactic designed to enhance its image, but the government

NATIONAL NETWORK TO END HUNGER-TRIBUTE TO WORK OF ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one does not have to wander too far from Parliament Hill to encounter the signs of hunger, even in affluent Ottawa. Along Bank and Sparks Streets, the sight of some poor soul eating out of a garbage can is not uncommon. And, less than a mile from Parliament Hill, St. Brigid's Soup Kitchen feeds the hungry 24 hours a day.
The problem of hunger stretches right across this huge country, from east to west and from north to south. It has many manifestations-children going to school without having breakfast, young mothers feeding their infants sugar water because they have no food in the house, and people who have not eaten for days, walking miles to food depots.
Thankfully, someone is doing something about the problem of hunger. The National Network to End Hunger grew out of the National Conference on Hunger in November, 1986. It is sponsored by a number of associations including churches, social workers, and other social development agencies. Their aim is to eliminate the need for food banks by 1992 by advocating policy improvements in areas such as housing, employment, and income security.
I hope I am speaking for all Members of Parliament, Mr. Speaker, when I salute the efforts of the National Network to End Hunger in Canada. Their efforts do not go unnoticed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Western Grain Stabilization Act has been a very helpful plan to grain and oilseed producers in this time of very low prices. We are considering amending the Act to make it easier for people who are not now part of the plan to participate. We are also considering increasing the levy to make the fund closer to being actuarily sound. We are also doing some other things which will make it more beneficial to producers.
I should also say that we are doing our calculations on the final payment for the previous crop year. It looks as though we will have a record amount of money available to producers for a final payment. That is good news which will be welcomed by producers when they see the size of the final payment.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
When I had to interrupt my remarks because the Oral Question Period was to begin at 11 a.m., Mr. Speaker, I was emphasizing some points in Bill C-86 and I was far from congratulating the Government for the substance of this piece of legislation.
One of the points I was about to make was that some provisions of this Bill are exceptionally harsh. Under these provisions, no individual who is convicted of an offence under the Act,-someone for instance who would oppose the continuation of the postal services-an offence that was committed while the individual was acting in the capacity of an officer or representative of the employer or the union shall be reinstated for a period of five years. Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is an excessive penalty.
There are already in this Bill very high fines for which the postal union, the Canada Post Corporation or even individuals could be liable, but this clause which would prevent an officer of the union or of Canada Post from getting his job back for a period of five years is excessive. I do not think that this clause is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. And I direct this question to the Government: Has the Government really done its work and obtained appropriate legal opinion to know for sure that this excessive penalty is consistent with the Charter of Rights?

I am afraid that the 5-year off-the-job penalty which would apply to either a senior officer of Canada Post or a senior officer of the union may contravene the Charter of Rights. I want an answer from the Government on whether this has
been checked, because I do not see a person not being able to do his or her job for a period of five years.
If an officer of Canada Post is not able to come back and work in his position for five years, where else will that person be able to work? It is a monopoly. There are no other post offices run in the country by the private sector. It is an extravagant penalty, and I want answers on whether or not it violates the Charter of Rights.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this Government, by introducing this back to work legislation, destroys our collective bargaining tradition. It simply wants to break the Canadian Union of Postal Workers in order to look tough with unions. It sees this as a means to score political points and halt its constant slipping in opinion polls.
Mr. Speaker, we shall not be party to a scheme whereby postal workers are held to ransom.

No legislation was needed to appoint the mediator who will be appointed under the provisions of this legislation. We have been calling for a mediator for over a week and the Government refused. What the Government should do now is what it should have done over a week ago, that is, appoint a mediator without the need for this legislation. The legislation should be put aside. It should be shelved. A mediator should be appointed in a climate without a sword of Damocles over both Canada Post and the union, so that the mediator can mediate in a reasonable way and with reasonable chances of success.
In conclusion, I have asked myself the following questions, and I should ask them of the Government. What has happened to democracy in the workplace? What is wrong with democracy in the workplace? What is wrong with the regular, bona fide negotiations which produced good results in the last letter carriers' strike in the month of June? How come the Government suddenly decided that what did work in the postal strike a few weeks ago will not work now?
These are the questions we are asking ourselves, and these are the questions we are asking the Government. These are the questions to which we want answers before we will support this piece of legislation.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) start the debate today, he implied that the legislation was similar to, if not the same as, the legislation introduced in August to order back the people who work on the railways. In fact, this legislation is significantly different. I believe that the Minister is deliberately trying to downplay or deny the aspects of this legislation. The legislation is so completely different that we must wonder why that is so and why the Minister is implying that it is not different.
Also, as I listened to his speech, I was asked by one of my colleagues whether he was still the Minister of Labour or the
October 9, 1987

Minister responsible for Canada Post. That is a significant question, because the speech was a management speech and the legislation is management legislation. There was absolutely no concern, no sympathy, no understanding of the employees affected by the piece of legislation.
Throughout the last number of months we listened to the Minister of Labour and he sounded more and more like the Minister responsible for Canada Post.
A decision of the Canada Labour Relations Board indicated that Canada Post was intimidating its workers and forcing them to do work which was normally done by employees on strike, and that it went against the Canada Labour Code. We asked the Minister to make a statement that that situation would no longer be tolerated, and he refused to do so. He said that the decision of the Canada Labour Relations Board with regard to two unionized workers in Halifax was enough.
I pointed out to him that I had talked with non-unionized employees who wanted some assurance from the Minister of Labour that Canada Post would follow the dictates of the Canada Labour Code. I asked the Minister whether he would rise and say that the Canada Labour Code indicates that workers cannot be intimidated into doing work which is being done by people who are on strike. He did not do that.
It is an impossible situation when we have a Minister of Labour who will not defend the labour legislation that is on the books and that has been on the books for many years. Employees do not expect the Minister of Labour to take their position on each and every occasion. But when it is clear that the employer is not obeying the law of the land, the Minister of Labour has the responsibilities of the Minister of Labour. He has failed in those responsibilities.
He has failed throughout the postal dispute to differentiate between his role as the Minister of Labour and his role as a member of Cabinet. This Cabinet has been Canada Post, one step removed. The answers we have had from the Minister responsible for Canada Post have been the answers of the management of Canada Post. It has been this Government which has refused to let the item that has caused the strike, the issue of franchising out those jobs, be negotiated.
Time after time when we have asked questions of the Minister responsible for Canada Post he has taken the position that this is a management issue. It is not a management issue. It is the issue which caused the strike. It is the issue of those people who are working in the wickets right across the country who want to maintain those jobs saying, "Look, we want to negotiate that point. We want to be in a position to try to secure the jobs that we have at the present time". That is a very legitimate reason for negotiating. To have the Minister responsible for Canada Post get up time after time and say that that is management's right, that that should not be negotiated, that it cannot be negotiated, meant that this strike was going to happen.
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
It is fine for the Government to say, "Well, the Foisy report basically supported management and therefore the union is wrong". That is not true. Unfortunately, again, one of the very aspects of this legislation that upsets us is that if the mediation does not work then the arbitrator, who is the same person, is instructed to look at the Foisy report. This is a report that is pro-management, a report that states that workers do not have the right to negotiate with management their present jobs. It is a report which obviously denies the whole idea of collective bargaining.
Someone else said that this is a conciliation officer who made the report and it is logical that the Government should say that the mediator or arbitrator should look at that report. If that is the case, why did the Government refuse to do that same thing in the case of the back-to-work legislation with regard to the railways? If one takes a look at Bill C-85, the legislation ordering the railway workers back to work, he will see that it does not tell the arbitrator to look at the conciliation report. Do you know why, Mr. Speaker? It is because the Government in that case did not like the conciliation report.
The unions said that it was the basis for negotiation. They said that there were items, not all of them, but a number of them in the conciliation report which made sense and which would help to resolve the items in dispute. We suggested to the same Minister of Labour that it may not be a bad idea to have a provision in the legislation that the conciliation report be referred directly to the arbitrator. But he would not do that. Now that there is a report that the Government likes, it is right in this legislation that the arbitrator must look at the Foisy report.
The Minister in his speech said that there has been a history of distrust between the employees at Canada Post, the unions involved, and the management. That is quite true. It has been a very difficult labour situation, historically. But what he is doing with this legislation is building up that distrust more and more. He is escalating the level of distrust.
For the first time ever the employees at Canada Post, the members of CUPW, have not had a general strike; they have not preached violence; they have had a rotating strike. They have encouraged their members not to be violent. They have done a very good job for the most part in making sure that that has been the case. They have allowed the mail to go through.
We even read in The Globe and Mail yesterday that this is not the time to order the postal workers back to work. I do not remember The Globe and Mail ever, historically, being a prolabour, pro-union newspaper. It recognized in its editorial yesterday that this was not 1978. It recognized that this was not some old fight between Canada Post and the postal workers, that there was a different regime and that this was a regime in which CUPW was trying to negotiate items. Its members were having a rotating strike. They were not asking for more. They were not trying to get a rich contract but trying to preserve the jobs that those men, and mainly those women, have at the present time.

October 9, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
As I indicated earlier, these jobs are decent-paying jobs, jobs which are held mainly by women. These are jobs which will, as a result of the Government's plan and Canada Post's proposals, be going out to drug stores, Bible book stores and to other stores across the nation where we know that the people hired will receive minimum wages. Basically, they will be women in part-time jobs with almost no extra benefits, no pension plan. There will be nothing other than the basics required by the law.
I have to ask why the Government believes that in 1987 when we have been talking about affirmative action for so long, when we have been talking about the fact that women are so often ghettoized in their jobs and why we have been so concerned with the fact that part-time workers do not have benefits, security and any sort of pension plan that is worth talking about, that its plan for franchising-out is forcing the creation of another job ghetto in this country. It has been argued that we need more service to the public. Post offices can stay open longer. It is being said that we are better off if we can go to our local store rather than to a post office building.
But take a look at where the franchising-out will be. In my constituency in the City of Thompson there is one post office. They have decided to franchise-out to three other stores. The City of Thompson is only two miles square. One of the post offices that has been set up is across the street from the main post office.
I have had a constituent talk to me already about this new improved service. He received one of those call-back cards telling him he had to go to this new subpost office, the one where minimum wages are paid. He went down to pick up his registered mail, but it was closed for inventory. Fine, so he went back to his car, saw that the post office was across the street, got out of his car, because he did not have to drive anywhere. He was told, "I am sorry, your letter is over at the subpost office, that is where you have to pick it up". It is closed for inventory, he could not do that. He came back the next day, it was open, they had finished their inventory but the woman who looks after the post office wicket was out. She was not there. So, again, the man who has parked his car right in front of the post office, has to leave because he cannot get his registered mail. Twice he has had to leave work, go and get his mail but could not do so because of the privatization plan. That is not an increase in service. It might be an increase in profits for that little book store but it is not an increase in service to the public of Canada.
It is being done deliberately by the Government, knowing full well that it is ruining any chance of labour peace within the Post Office. It knows at the same time that it is forcing women to give up jobs that they have had, which they have had to work many years to get, those so-called preferable jobs at the wickets. Those jobs will now disappear.
The Government says they can take other jobs. It is quite willing to make sure no one is fired as a result of this situation. Yet as you take away those two wicket jobs in one town, three in another, four in the next, because they have all been sent out to sub post offices, those women will have to take evening jobs or jobs in other communities because there is no guarantee we will need more mail sorters in those small towns and cities. Yes, this will not cost anyone their jobs, but it will make it damn difficult for them to keep working. The Government knows that is true but is too blind to admit it.
This strike was provoked by the two Ministers sitting across from me. They are the cause and that is why we cannot expedite passage of this legislation. In other cases of such legislation, even though we have not liked it, even though we thought it was basically unfair, we have worked to see it passed in all stages in two or three days, sometimes even less. We did that because we believe the Government has the right to intervene at some point to re-establish essential services, if that be the case. Even though we have not liked the legislation, and quite often we have been morally offended by what was in it, we have co-operated. Yet today both opposition Parties got up and said that we are not co-operating because the Government is causing an unnecessary dispute. It is causing grief for families right across this country. It is taking jobs away from women, and it is all completely unnecessary.
I believe this is part of a political agenda by a Government which has to prove it can beat someone, somewhere, sometime. It needs this for its psychological make-up, and to keep its right-wing back-benchers happy. No one else really believes we have to take away those wicket jobs. No one else accepts the Government, through Canada Post, saying day after day that this cannot be negotiated. It does not matter that the union has conceded that in such situations these sub post offices can be set up. It does not matter that there has been a willingness to negotiate and recognize that this is going to happen to some degree. The unions recognize the role of management but they want the right to sit down with management and negotiate major items of contention. They are concerned with the security of the jobs of the people they represent. They are concerned with the right of people not to be forced to move to other centres because that is the only way they can work for Canada Post.
I anticipate that some government Members will eventually want to get up and say, well, things change with time. You cannot always live in the 18th century. That is not the issue here. We are not talking about new technology taking away jobs. We are talking about these jobs being done by private enterprise, not by public enterprise. We are talking about the jobs being done at less than decent wages. They cannot be done by women who want regular employment.
I cannot for the life of me understand, apart from its political paranoia, why the Government will not allow this item to be negotiated. Is it so important to the Minister
October 9, 1987

responsible for Canada Post, the Minister of Labour, and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour that these positions be posted out and the jobs become part-time? Is it so important that they cannot negotiate? I cannot understand why they take that attitude.
1 would like to get back to some of the other items in this legislation, which is not the same as the back-to-work legislation in the case of the railway workers. That is important because, as I said earlier, the Minister of Labour tried to impress the media with the fact that the legislation is basically the same. I have already pointed out the different way the conciliation report is being handled. Because the Government likes it, the arbitrator has to look at it. In the railway legislation the Government did not like the conciliation report so it was not referred to the arbitrator.
Then the Government says it sent in a mediator. People should not worry about that. Yes, the union called for a mediator. Yes, the two opposition Parties called for a mediator. Yet you look at the legislation and we have a mediator-arbitrator, the same person for both functions. That person will have to act as a mediator for two months and, if things do not work out, will have to switch hats and become an arbitrator. Talk about built-in failure.
The whole concept of a mediator, as anyone involved in collective bargaining knows, is that it is someone both sides can trust as an honest broker. It is someone sitting down in confidence and saying we are willing to move this way if the other side will move here. We will give if they do not take as much. This is a real problem and this is what has to be resolved. A mediator cannot fulfil that function if at the same time he acts as the arbitrator.
The role of an arbitrator is the opposite to that of a mediator. The arbitrator is to listen to formal presentations and then make a decision. Canada Post, the Government in disguise, and the workers through their union are not going to be able to work with that mediator the way they should be able to because, for political gimmickry, we have a mediator who becomes an arbitrator so the Government can go to the public and the media and say we were asked to provide a mediator, we were asked to let negotiations take place, and we have done that. It has not. It has sabotaged them. Not only that, it has increased the amount of distrust the workers have for the Government.
I ask the Minister, why not have a mediator who works for two months and then have someone else go in if the negotiations have not succeeded? Why not allow mediation to work? Why kill it in advance? I have heard so many speeches by the Minister saying it is always best to try and negotiate and that he is giving the two parties one more opportunity to solve the issue at the table before arbitration comes in.

That requirement has been included in a lot of back-to-work legislation. However, the clause which says that employees, officials or elected people of the union who disobey the law are automatically barred from their job or elected position for the next five years is unjust. It was not put in the back-to-work legislation for the railway workers. At that time the Minister of Labour said that he did not believe it was a just clause. But now it is a just clause. In a Cabinet that has had such legal problems, even if one or two former Ministers were convicted and went to jail or had to pay financial penalties, they still in spite of that retain the right to run for election.

October 9, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
The right that former Cabinet Ministers have to be re-elected is being denied to shop stewards. It is a very unusual, severe and unjust penalty, a penalty which the Minister did not think was necessary in the case of the railway workers.
There is always the question of credibility with the Government. I believe that that is the essence of the problem here. People believe that the Minister of Labour should be acting impartially. He should not be the management representative and he should not, after a certain level, be the representative of the workers. Decisions are supposed to be impartial, but I do not think that that has ever happened here when there have been disputes in the past at the Post Office. In a letter written on July 29, 1987 the P.M. said:
We all recognize that labour relations at Canada Post have had a turbulent history. A long-term solution to these problems can only be worked out by the corporation and its unions through compromise and a willingness to work toward establishing a mature labour-management relationship. Government intervention has not been the solution to labour disputes in the past and is unlikely to be the panacea of the future.
When you get a letter like that from the Prime Minister you have to believe that he is advocating negotiations, advocating, to use his own word, compromise, and he is saying that the best solution is obviously not back-to-work legislation. The Government will not allow negotiations on the primary item, the issue of franchising out. That has been said time after time by Ministers of the Crown. The Government will not allow compromise and is forcing the situation where we have to have back-to-work legislation, something which the Prime Minister said is not a benefit and will not be a benefit in labour relations of Canada Post.
The situation involves a strike caused by Government, for unjust reasons, affecting families right across the country. Yet the Government expects us in the House to be a rubber stamp for its political agenda.
I was actually quite proud of the way in which the postal workers handled the strike. I was happy and very pleased to see how limited was the violence. I know it is not easy. I come from a town where they have actually built log cabins right on a provincial highway to discourage people from crossing a picket line. Unfortunately the people have taken shots at the helicopters and the union has had to stop them. I know how high emotions can run strong when strike breakers or scabs are brought in. I know how strong those emotions are and how difficult it is to try to keep a tight rein on that type of situation. For the most part we have seen success, but if there is any increase in violence now it will not be as a result of a change in strategy by the union, but as a result of unjust, unfair and unnecessary legislation being forced upon the employees by Government, which is management in this case. How can people feel that they are being treated fairly when their jobs are disappearing, when the Government will not negotiate the item about which they are concerned and when the Government uses its power to order people back to work by legislation
that is much more harsh, restrictive and balanced in favour of management than has been other legislation introduced in this House to order people back to work?
If the union and its members know that the Government will use its legislative clout to deny them basic rights, of course violence will increase, even though we all deplore it. It also means that in the future it will be very hard to convince working men and women, not only at Canada Post but in other Crown corporations, that they will be treated fairly. It is a bad sign and a bad signal. It is an indication that when people are negotiating with Air Canada, the Canadian National Railways, or with the federal Government itself, they will not be treated fairly, that their concerns are not concerns that can be dealt with in negotiations because the Government will not allow it. If negotiations are not settled, even though they are not allowed to negotiate items important to them, the Government will in the end introduce legislation, wording it in such a way that it benefits the management side. That has obviously happened here. The penalty clauses are aimed not at management but at the employees.
The reference of the Foisy report is again one which management wanted and the Government wanted. Yet it was not done in the railway legislation when the union wanted the same thing. The request for an independent mediator, something that is allowed under Canadian law, something that the Minister of Labour is allowed to do, was not agreed to despite the fact that union asked for it, despite the fact that the two Opposition Parties asked for it, and despite the fact that a lot of groups in our society believed it was a good idea Because Canada Post did not believe it was a good idea, it was not done, and that is the truth.
This was and remains a strike caused by the Government. It is unjust for the House of Commons to pass this legislation, and it is certainly unjust for the House of Commons to pass it quickly. We will oppose this legislation. Later on, we will seek to amend the legislation.
As long as the Government refuses to change the legislation, and as long as the Government refuses to allow working men and women to negotiate for some semblance of job security, then we will have to oppose the legislation.

subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to make a few observations relating to Bill C-86, the Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987, and the developments which gave rise to the necessity for a legislated end to the current postal dispute. I want to say most emphatically to all Hon. Members present that I believe that this Bill should be supported for two very important reasons.
October 9, 1987

The first reason is that, in view of current developments in the dispute and the fact that the parties have failed to resolve their differences since their last agreement expired more than a year ago, the Goverment has little alternative but to restore full postal operations through legislative means. The second reason as to why I feel that the legislation should be supported lies in the merits of the method of dispute settlement provided for in the Bill now before us. The selection of mediation-arbitration as the dispute settlement mechanism is well suited to this particular dispute and I believe that it deserves the endorsement of all Hon. Members.
I think that it would be appropriate to review the background to the current dispute if only to provide some insight into the extensive third-party efforts which have been made over a lengthy period of time in an attempt to bring about a peaceful conclusion. The collective agreement between Canada Post Corporation and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers expired September 30, 1986, and conciliation efforts began one month later with the appointment of conciliation officer Andre Drouin of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service of Labour Canada. Mr. Drouin held meetings with union and management negotiators over a three-month period but there was little progress made in resolving any of the issues in dispute.
Mr. Claude Foisy was subsequently appointed as conciliation commissioner in the dispute on February 23, 1987, and numerous meetings were held between the commissioner and the parties over the period from March 2nd through August 12th. As we heard the Minister of Labour say earlier in this debate, Mr. Foisy is an experienced labour relations practitioner and a former Vice-Chairman of the Canada Labour Relations Board. Unfortunaly, the parties saw fit not to draw on the knowledge and abilities of the commissioner in achieving a settlement but rather to bury him in position papers and briefing notes. Discussions for the most part were limited to exchanges on principles and rarely came to grips with the specifics relating to the operative sections of the contract. Mr. Foisy went so far as to suggest that if the parties are not happy with the proposed wording of certain recommandations, then "they have only themselves to blame, having had over Five months to give me their comments".
One can appreciate the frustration which the conciliation commissioner must have felt in attempting to elicit meaningful dialogue from the parties and instead being faced with two sides more intent on avoiding their responsibilities to make use of the collective bargaining process. The commissioner's report, a comprehensive document comprising some 82 pages, was released to the parties on September 22. Post-conciliation meetings were held between the parties, but again they involved more public posturing than actual bargaining. On
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
September 29th, the Minister of Labour asked his Associate Deputy Minister, Bill Kelly, to meet with the parties to assess the chances of a negotiated settlement, either in direct negotiations or with the assistance of a mediator. By all accounts, this assessment was quite negative as to the prospects for a negotiated settlement short of a protracted work stoppage. In a telegram dated October 6, 1987, the Minister gave the parties one further opportunity to settle their differences. He warned them that whether a Bill would be introduced or not depended on their will and capacity to achieve resolution through the collective bargaining process. However, despite all of these opportunities, the differences between the positions of the parties on several major issues have made any hope of a near term settlement next to impossible.
Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members are only too well aware of the serious consequences which a work stoppage of this nature can have on Canadian businesses which are dependent upon the postal service for their economic survival. The citizens of Canada do not deserve to be subjected to a second disruption of their mail sevice. With no hope of a negotiated settlement in sight, this Government has taken its responsibility to the Canadian people to restore full postal service, with provision for the settlement of the issues in dispute through mediation or arbitration.
Mr. Speaker, the Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987, provides for the immediate termination of the current work stoppage and a resumption of full postal operations. The legislation also extends the collective agreement for a period to be determined through arbitration of not less than two and not more than three years. Perhaps, most importantly, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that this legislation provides for the settlement of the parties' differences through the process of mediation-arbitration or "med-arb" as it is more commonly referred to in labour relations terminology.
1 think that it is important that Hon. Members appreciate the rationale which the Minister of Labour has used in providing for the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator to deal with the resolution of the issues in dispute between Canada Post Corporation and CUPW. Basically, Mr. Speaker, what this piece of legislation provides is a last opportunity for the two sides to roll up their sleeves and get down to serious bargaining or face the prospect of having a third party make binding decisions which will dictate the details of any new collective agreement. I am sure that Hon. Members would agree that legislative solutions cannot possibly address all of the problems and frustrations which need to be worked out at the bargaining table. This is why it is imperative that the parties seize this opportunity to work with the mediator to arrive at a mutually acceptable agreement.

October 9, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
Under the med-arb procedure provided for in the legislation before us today, the two sides to the dispute, while party to an arbitration proceeding, still have the opportunity to carry out the negotiation process. The mediator-arbitrator combines the skills and functions of the mediator with an ultimate mandate to make a final and binding decision on all issues which cannot be mediated to resolution. The influence of the mediator-arbitrator on the outcome of negotiations is more than that of a conventional mediator because the parties are aware that, if they fail to reach agreement, the same person will be switching roles to that of arbitrator and rendering a binding decision.
The process of mediation-arbitration has been used on a limited basis in the federal jurisdiction before, and has proven its worth as one of the more promising alternatives which exist for the resolution of collective bargaining disputes. In this particular instance, we can only hope that it will prove effective in prompting Canada Post and CUPW into coming to grips with those issues which are preventing the achievement of a new collective agreement. In addition to having the opportunity to meet with the parties and gain a full appreciation for the issues and the distance separating them on specific items, the mediator-arbitrator appointed under this legislation will have the benefit of the extensive evaluation of he dispute already undertaken by conciliation commissioner Claude Foisy and fully documented in his report.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would reiterate my concern that this Bill, the Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987, receive prompt passage by Hon. Members so that the confrontation between Canada Post and CUPW can be terminated as soon as possible. Critics of back to work legislation often suggest that one of the more dangerous consequences of legislative intervention in the collective bargaining process is the potential which is created for disrespect of the rule of law. For any legislation to be respected, it must be perceived as just and fair. While a personally find the requirement to introduce this particular legislation to be unfortunate, I applaud the enlightened approach which the minister of labour has adopted in the Bill with regard to the dispute resolution mechanism. Not only does the proposed legislation provide the parties to the dispute with one last opportunity to resolve their differences themselves, but the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator requires the parties to approach the process in a constructive and responsible manner, to ensure full consideration of their respective contract proposals.
I urge all Hon. Members to support the Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking in the debate on Bill C-86 this afternoon, my colleage the Hon. Member for Montreal-Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) clearly described the situation and the dangers which may result from a government which is clearly seeking a confrontation with its employees and whose attitude is responsible for the current postal strike.
I would not want to repeat what he said, but I should like especially to address the following questions: Why is there a strike? How did we get there, Mr. Speaker? After a period of five years with no strike, how is it that we are now faced with a second strike in two months?
First, Mr. Speaker, we should go back a few years. Of course, we all remember and Canadians all remember that the

October 9, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
1960's were not easy years. We went through a period of changes, of automation, and of course at that time we experienced very extensive labour disputes that were very wearisome for everybody. And it was a Liberal Government in 1981 that established the Canada Post Corporation, with three specific mandates, Mr. Speaker-first, to improve employer-employee labour relations; second, to improve services; and third, to reduce the deficit.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, those three mandates have equal priority. There were not one, two or three that had to be met by steps. But the three mandates were an overall mandate for Canada Post Corporation to provide Canadians with better services, reduce its deficit rather than constantly digging into Government coffers, and third, of course, to enjoy labour relations that would allow the Corporation to provide good services.
But, in 1984, there was a changeover in government, Mr. Speaker. And this Government, with a legitimate mandate from the people, decided once again to conduct a study of Canada Post Corporation. Indeed, in June 1985, the former Minister in charge of Canada Post Corporation set up the Review Committee to consider the terms of reference and productivity of Canada Post Corporation, which was to be known as the Marchment Committee.
Here we are in the House today debating a Bill which does away with the right to strike and forces the union membership back to work, yet the issue is not higher wages but job security. Mr. Speaker, the whole matter revolves around the privatization of Canada Post. From the outset, Mr. Speaker, I should like to focus on the danger and the problem which even the Marchment Committee envisioned if the Government were to give serious consideration to the possibility of privatizing Canada Post.
In the report-page 23 in French, page 20 in English-the committee looked at two privatization avenues. The first one was to sell Canada Post lock, stock and barrel, so then the whole thing would have been in the private sector. The committee did consider whether or not this would be practical, and I should like to read a paragraph concerning this option, on page 20 of the report.
"There is, however, one difficulty which the Committee is convinced could not be overcome at this time. The Post Office's continuing history of annual losses makes it an unattractive candidate fpr sale in its entirety as a going concern. Even if it were given away, the newly established corporation with no history of prior earnings would find it virtually impossible to arrange adequate financing in the private money markets. To turn the Canada Post over to the private sector and then provide the new corporation with Government grants and guarantees would hardly satisfy the objective of reducing the real and potential drain on the Treasury and, hence, on the taxpayer."
As indicated in this paragraph the committee clearly states that selling the whole Canada Post operations to the private sector was unthinkable. And then there is the second option. Here is the following paragraph on page 20, Mr. Speaker.
"The second approach to privatization is to sell it off in parts. No doubt, if the Government decided to withdraw from the postal business on a phased basis, there would be many bids to take over heavily populated areas which generate high postal revenues. However, areas of the country which are thinly populated and lack industrial concentration would be less attractive to business.
These areas do not now generate sufficient postal revenue to cover the cost of mail processing and delivery. Some form of transfer payments would be imperative to make servicing of such areas viable. Indeed, it may well prove necessary to keep a much reduced Canada Post in existence as the mail handler of last resort. Such a Post Office would, of necessity, be an ongoing charge against public funds. The Committee is of the view that so long as universality of postal service is accepted as a tenet of public policy, privatization by parts is not the most desirable solution. Far better to turnaround the present Crown corporation and make it self-sufficient. The Committee is convinced that this can be done.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on the record recommendation no. 10 that the Marchment Committee has made on the privatization of Canada Post: "That privatization not be considered at this time. However, if Canada Post fails by 1990 to achieve its objectives of service and financial self-sufficiency, privatization should then be re-considered."
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues may wonder why I just read that recommendation, which is found on page 20 of the Marchment report.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that a strike has been called and we have to debate back-to-work legislation for the postal workers precisely because the Government wants to privatize the Canada Post Corporation. The Government chose the second option discussed by the Marchment Committee, which was to do this progressively. The Canada Post Corporation presented its corporate plan in November 1986 following the instructions it had received from by the Minister of Finance in February 1986. The Minister had said: From now on, you will have to be self-sufficient and you will not receive one cent in subsidies after March 31, 1988, at the beginning of the new fiscal year. This is when the Canada Post Corporation developed an action plan in three specific stages. These are mentioned in the report.
First, Canada Post began with the rural regions. Everyone will remember this, and I am certain that the Conservative Members who represent a rural region will remember it because they travelled throughout the country and there were demonstrations, meetings and petitions. Since there was so much pressure, they went before the Committee which was discussing the corporate plan of Canada Post, and because of the number of Conservative Members from rural regions, the
October 9, 1987

Government had to soften its approach, but it never abandoned its plan of closing as many rural post offices as possible because they are not profitable.
The second option was to install superboxes everywhere so that Canada Post would be able to leave mail delivery to subcontractors, and this resulted in a lettercarrier strike in June. The strike lasted ten days and there were acts of violence. And at the request of all parties, a mediator was appointed and it took him two days to settle the matter.
The third option, Mr. Speaker, is privatization, that is selling postal stations of franchising to the private sector. As indicated in the Marchment Report, that option is not workable, it is not a good idea. But it is being done precisely because it is easier to transfer postal services to the private sector because in urban areas there are many people and businesses and it will therefore be possible to maintain the service. That is why two strikes occurred within the past three months and that is the reason for the present one, Mr. Speaker.
Therefore, when you say that the minister provides in the legislation for the appointment of a mediator and arbitrator afterwards, it should be noted as well, Mr. Speaker, that at the same time the mediator is given the mandate to say: You must pursue bargaining according to the report of the conciliator who at that time agreed with Canada Post Corporation, which was entitled to sell those postal stations.
